results.problem: The rendering omits nirupamarasam, which describes the bone as having incomparable flavour, in addition to saying that the dog eats it with relish.
results.sanskrit_says: The dog gladly eats a meatless human bone that is worm-covered, saliva-soaked, foul-smelling and disgusting, yet of incomparable flavour; it does not heed even Indra nearby, since a petty creature does not recognize the worthlessness of its possession.

results.problem: The supplied Sanskrit has vacanena, “speech” or “words,” not kavacena, “armour”; the English silently follows a different reading.
results.sanskrit_says: As the text stands, it asks: “If there is forbearance, what need is there of speech?” The remaining comparisons are rendered correctly.

results.problem: The English omits the epithet viṣṭapahārin, “taker-away or destroyer of the world,” applied to Hari.
results.sanskrit_says: All the listed blessings are obtained when wish-granting Hari, the taker-away of the world, is pleased.

results.problem: “Careless spending” merges two separate causes, tyāga and pramāda, and therefore omits their distinction.
results.sanskrit_says: Wealth is ruined through relinquishing or giving it away and through negligence or carelessness.

results.problem: “When full” misleadingly suggests physical satiety; sampūrṇa here contrasts with destitution and means having become prosperous or wealthy.
results.sanskrit_says: A destitute person longs for a handful of barley, but after becoming prosperous regards the entire earth as no more valuable than grass.
